mainTopic: Proof for documents in a family manager's name, and two kinds of חזקה: three years with a claim versus a quick act of acquiring
overview: This amud finishes the discussion of a brother who runs the shared family business and holds documents in his own name. A challenge to רב's concession, based on a ruling of רב הונא בר אבין, stays unanswered (קשיא). רב חסדא limits רב's ruling to brothers who share even their food. רבה says the proof must come from witnesses, while רב ששת says confirming the document is enough. רב נחמן answers רבא's question by quoting a ברייתא: both the brother and a widow who runs the household must bring proof, even though the widow is praised for working hard for the orphans. The גמרא then turns to the משנה's line about gifts and brothers who divide. It explains that a חזקה backed by a claim needs three years, but a חזקה with no claim works at once through a small act like locking or fencing. Finally, רבא explains that רב הושעיא's 'in his presence' means the seller does not need to say 'Go, take hold and acquire,' and his explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Challenge from the rule about items that are usually lent or rented
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב's concession about the case where the brother died. It cites רב הונא בר אבין: a person holding items that are usually lent or rented is not believed when he says he bought them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב הונא בר אבין sent: if someone holds items that people usually lend or rent out, and he says 'I bought them,' he is not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ruling from רב הונא בר אבין to attack רב's concession. רב agreed that if the brother died, his orphans do not have to bring proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding something is normally a sign of ownership. That sign is weak when the item is the kind of thing that passes from hand to hand. The documents here are like such items, so the brother could not keep them without proof, and his orphans should be no better off than he was.

keyTerms.meaning: as he sent (a ruling sent in a letter)
items that are usually lent or rented out

phrases.english: As Rav Huna bar Avin sent:
Items that are usually lent and rented out,
and he said, 'They are bought and in my hand,'
he is not believed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier challenge against רב's concession that if the brother died, the burden of proof moves to the other brothers.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's concession that the dead brother's orphans do not need to bring proof
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Items that are usually lent or rented give their holder no believable claim of ownership. So the father needed proof, and his orphans, who only stand in his place, should need proof too.

steps.title: The challenge stands unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא admits it has no answer: קשיא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits that the challenge against רב's concession has no answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying קשיא means the question stays open. It does not fully reject the opinion. The גמרא simply admits it cannot resolve the problem and moves on.

keyTerms.meaning: it is difficult; the question stands unresolved

phrases.english: It is difficult.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the challenge of step 1 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The challenge to רב's concession in the case where the brother died remains unanswered.

steps.title: רב חסדא limits רב's ruling to brothers who share even their food
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says the brother must bring proof only when the brothers share everything, even their dough. If they keep separate food budgets, he could have saved money from his own portion.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: this was taught only when the brothers do not divide even their dough. But if they do divide their dough, say that he saved it from his own dough.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא narrows the ruling that the brother must bring proof. It applies only to brothers who share absolutely everything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the brothers share even their food, all money is shared, so anything in his name probably came from the common pot. If each brother eats from his own portion, he could have spent less on food and saved his own money. Then his claim that the property is his makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: they taught this only in a case where
divided in their dough, meaning they keep separate food

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that who must bring proof depends on how closely the brothers actually share their money.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא דְּאֵין חֲלוּקִין בְּעִיסָּתָן,
phrases.english: They taught this only when they are not divided even in their dough,
phrases.notes: 'This' is רב's ruling that the brother has to bring proof.

phrases.english: but if they are divided in their dough,
say that he saved it from his own dough.
phrases.notes: He means he ate less and put away the money he saved.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the unanswered challenge back to the main ruling and defines when it applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The brother must bring proof only when the brothers share even their food. If they eat separately, we assume he could have saved his own money.

steps.title: What kind of proof is needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what counts as the 'proof' the brother must bring.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question to set up the next step. When we say 'bring proof,' what exactly does he have to bring?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now we only heard that someone must bring proof. This question looks for the exact standard of evidence that will satisfy the court.

phrases.english: Proof: with what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the word 'proof' in the ruling being discussed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of evidence counts as proof that the property belongs to the brother?

steps.title: רבה says witnesses; רב ששת says confirming the document
steps.stepSummary: רבה says proof means witnesses. רב ששת says proof means the court's confirmation of the document.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: proof with witnesses. רב ששת said: proof with confirming the document.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer the question in different ways. רבה demands witnesses, and רב ששת is satisfied with confirming the document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבה, the brother needs witnesses that the money or property is really his, for example that he inherited it. For רב ששת, it is enough to confirm that the document bearing his name is valid. That is an easier standard to meet.

keyTerms.meaning: the court's confirmation that a document is valid

phrases.english: Rabba said: proof with witnesses,

phrases.aramaic: רַב שֵׁשֶׁת אָמַר: רְאָיָה בְּקִיּוּם הַשְּׁטָר.
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said: proof with confirming the document.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבה: proof through witnesses. רב ששת: proof through the court confirming the document.

steps.title: רבא asks רב נחמן which opinions he follows
steps.stepSummary: רבא lists both disputes, רב against שמואל and רבה against רב ששת. He asks רב נחמן whose side he takes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רב נחמן: here is רב and here is שמואל, here is רבה and here is רב ששת. Master, whom do you agree with?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא sums up the two disputes and asks רב נחמן for his ruling. This sets up רב נחמן's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate questions. The first is who must bring proof, which is the dispute of רב and שמואל. The second is what kind of proof is needed, which is the dispute of רבה and רב ששת. רבא wants רב נחמן's position on both.

phrases.english: Rava said to Rav Nachman:
Here is Rav and here is Shmuel,
here is Rabba and here is Rav Sheshet;
Master, whom do you agree with?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַב נַחְמָן: הָא רַב וְהָא שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a ruling on the disputes laid out in the earlier steps.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רב נחמן follow רב or שמואל on who must bring proof, and רבה or רב ששת on what kind of proof is needed?

steps.title: רב נחמן answers by quoting a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says he relies on a ברייתא. It teaches that a brother who runs the household business and claims the documents in his name came from his mother's father must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I know a ברייתא, as it was taught: one of the brothers who was doing business in the house, and bills of sale and documents were going out in his name, and he said 'They are mine; they came to me as an inheritance from my mother's father's house,' he must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן does not give his own reasoning. He quotes a ברייתא that rules in the case under discussion. The ברייתא continues past this line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ruling of the ברייתא puts the burden of proof on the brother himself, which matches רב's view. Since a ברייתא carries more weight than an אמורא's opinion, רב נחמן is using it to show which side is correct.

keyTerms.meaning: a ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the תנאים

steps.confusionAlert: The phrase 'my mother's father' matters. The brothers have the same father but different mothers. So this inheritance would belong to him alone, and that is why he claims the property is his.

phrases.english: He said to him: I know a baraita,
as it was taught: one of the brothers
who was doing business within the household,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָיוּ אוֹנוֹת וּשְׁטָרוֹת יוֹצְאִין עַל שְׁמוֹ,
phrases.english: and bills of sale and documents were going out in his name,
and he said: 'They are mine,'
'for they came to me from the house of my mother's father,'
it is upon him to bring proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins רב נחמן's answer to רבא's question by quoting a ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב נחמן relies on a ברייתא. Its first ruling, quoted so far, puts the burden of proof on the brother himself, like רב.
steps.raayaObject: Which view is correct in the dispute about who must bring proof
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a brother who did business in the household

steps.title: The ברייתא continues with the widow's case
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that a woman who runs the household business and claims the documents in her name came from her own family must also bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: Likewise, a woman who does business in the house, with bills of sale and documents in her name, who says 'They are mine, I inherited them from my father's father or my mother's father,' must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא that רב נחמן quoted keeps going with a second, parallel case: a woman running the household business.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like the brother in step 7, a document in her name is not enough to show the property is really hers. She could have bought it with estate money and put her own name on it. So she has to bring proof.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is still the source רב נחמן uses to choose a side. Because it requires proof, it lines up with the view that the person running the business is not believed just because the papers carry his or her name.

phrases.english: And similarly, the woman
phrases.notes: She is a widow running the house with her late husband's property, as the lines about orphans in step 10 show.

phrases.english: who does business inside the house,
and there were bills of sale and documents
going out in her name,
and she said: They are mine,
for they came to me from the house of my father's father
or from the house of my mother's father,
it is upon her to bring proof.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן הָאִשָּׁה שֶׁהִיא נוֹשֵׂאת וְנוֹתֶנֶת בְּתוֹךְ הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted by רב נחמן, adding a parallel case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A widow who runs the business also needs proof that the documents in her name are hers.

steps.title: Why does the ברייתא need the word 'and similarly'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the woman's case adds, since it seems to be the same as the brother's case.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the point of 'and similarly'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא bothered to repeat the same rule for the woman. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the rule for the woman is exactly the same as for the brother, the second case looks extra. The גמרא assumes every case in a ברייתא teaches something new, so it looks for what that is.

phrases.english: What is the point of "and similarly"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the ברייתא needed the second case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What new idea does the woman's case teach beyond the brother's case?

steps.title: We might have trusted her because she cares for the orphans
steps.stepSummary: Without this case, we might think the woman is believed, since people praise her for working hard for the orphans and assume she would not steal from them. The ברייתא teaches that she still needs proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that a woman, since she gains a good name when people say 'She works hard for the orphans,' would not steal from the orphans. The ברייתא teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the woman's case adds: even someone who seems trustworthy to everyone still needs proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The brother's case alone would not teach this, because a brother has no special reputation to protect. The woman's good name might have made us trust her. The ברייתא rules that a good reputation does not replace proof.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter is praiseworthy for her
It teaches us (that this is not so)

steps.whatToRemember: The woman's case teaches that even a person with a good reputation for caring for the orphans must bring proof. Documents in her name are not enough.

phrases.english: You might have said: a woman,
since the matter brings her praise,
because people say: She works hard for the orphans,
she would not steal from the orphans;
so it teaches us that she still needs proof.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The woman's case teaches that her good reputation does not make her believed without proof.

steps.title: The משנה's line about gifts and brothers dividing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now quotes the משנה: the three-year rule applies to a מחזיק, but a gift or brothers dividing work differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: In what case is this said? With one who holds possession. But with one who gives a gift, or brothers who divided, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new section of the משנה and quotes it. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה seems to say the three-year rule is only for a מחזיק. For a gift or brothers splitting an estate, a simple act like locking a door or fencing is enough to take ownership right away.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case are these words said?
One who holds and uses property

phrases.english: In what case is this said?
With one who holds possession,
but with one who gives a gift
and brothers who divided, and so on.
phrases.notes: The rest of the משנה says that in these cases, locking a door or fencing even a little counts as taking ownership.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic by quoting the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three-year rule is said about a מחזיק. A gift or brothers dividing work through a quick act of taking ownership.

steps.title: Are the gift and brothers cases not חזקה too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה's wording. By setting 'מחזיק' against a gift, brothers dividing and a גר's property, the משנה sounds as if those cases are not חזקה. Yet they are also acquired by taking hold.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say that all those we mentioned before are not cases of חזקה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the משנה's wording sounds wrong. This challenge sets up the fix in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה contrasts 'מחזיק' with gifts and brothers dividing. But a gift or a split is also a kind of חזקה, since locking or fencing is itself an act of taking hold. So the contrast as written does not make sense.

phrases.english: Is that to say that all these we mentioned,
are not cases of חזקה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of the משנה just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's contrast between 'מחזיק' and the gift and brothers cases.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Locking or fencing is also a kind of חזקה, so the משנה cannot mean those cases have nothing to do with חזקה.

steps.title: The משנה is missing words: a חזקה that comes with a claim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה left out words. It means the three-year rule is for a חזקה backed by a claim, like a seller and buyer arguing over a sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is missing words, and this is what it teaches: In what case is this said? With a חזקה that comes with a claim, for example the seller says 'I did not sell' and the buyer says 'I bought.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the משנה by adding the missing words. The full fixed wording keeps going after this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The contrast is not 'חזקה' against 'no חזקה.' It is between two kinds: a three-year חזקה that serves as evidence in a dispute, and a quick act of taking ownership in a gift or a split. The three-year kind applies when there is an argument, such as a seller denying the sale.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what it teaches
A חזקה that comes with a claim

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the gift and brothers cases have no חזקה. It is saying they use a different kind of חזקה than the three-year kind used to prove ownership in an argument.

phrases.english: It is missing words,
and this is what it teaches:
In what case is this said?
With a חזקה that comes with a claim,
for example, the seller says: "I did not sell,"
and the buyer says: "I bought";

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12 by adding missing words to the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Fixing the text by adding missing words (חסורי מחסרא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to say the gift and brothers cases have nothing to do with חזקה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is contrasting a three-year חזקה backed by a claim with a quick act of taking ownership in a gift or a split.

steps.title: Without a claim, a small act of acquiring is enough
steps.stepSummary: The reworded משנה goes on: a חזקה with no claim, like a gift, brothers dividing, or a גר's property, is only a way to acquire. Locking, fencing, or breaching even a little works right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a חזקה that has no claim with it, such as one who gives a gift, brothers who divide, or someone who takes hold of a גר's property, is just a way of acquiring. If he locked, fenced, or breached even a little, that is a חזקה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the reworded reading of the משנה it started in the last step. It shows the second kind of חזקה, the kind with no claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here nobody is arguing about who owns the land. The giver, the brothers, or the empty status of a גר's estate all agree the land can go to this person. So the act is not proof of ownership. It is simply the way to take ownership, and one small act does it with no three years needed.

keyTerms.meaning: A חזקה with no claim attached, where nobody is arguing about ownership
The property of a גר who died without Jewish heirs, so it belongs to no one and anyone can take it
Locked, fenced, breached: small physical acts that show ownership

steps.whatToRemember: There are two kinds of חזקה. A חזקה with a claim (a seller and buyer arguing) needs three years as proof. A חזקה with no claim (a gift, brothers dividing, a גר's property) is just an act of acquiring and works at once with even a small act.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two kinds of חזקה. In the three-year kind, the act is evidence of ownership. In this kind, the act itself is what makes him the owner.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the משנה treated a gift and brothers dividing differently from all the earlier three-year cases.

phrases.english: But a חזקה that has no claim with it –
such as one who gives a gift,
and brothers who divided,
and one who takes hold of the property of a convert –
phrases.notes: This is a גר who died without heirs, so his property belongs to no one and anyone can take it.

phrases.english: where it is simply for acquiring;
if he locked, fenced, or breached even a little –
this is a חזקה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the reworded reading of the משנה that step 13 began
steps.terutzResolutionType: Missing words added to the משנה (חסורי מחסרא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to say that a gift, brothers dividing and a גר's property have nothing to do with חזקה.
steps.terutzMaskana: There are two kinds of חזקה: one with a claim, which needs three years, and one with no claim, which works at once through a small act.

steps.title: רב הושעיא's ברייתא adds 'in his presence'
steps.stepSummary: רב הושעיא quotes a ברייתא from the school of לוי: locking, fencing, or breaching even a little, in his presence, is a חזקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הושעיא taught in the קידושין collection of the school of לוי: if he locked, fenced, or breached even a little in his presence, that is a חזקה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that repeats the same rule about small acts, but adds the words 'in his presence.' This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new detail is בפניו, meaning in front of the seller or giver. The ברייתא seems to make his presence a condition for the act to work.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who quotes this ברייתא
A collection of ברייתות about acquiring, taught in the study hall of לוי
In his presence, meaning in front of the seller

phrases.english: Rav Hoshaya taught
in the Kiddushin collection of the school of Levi:
phrases.notes: This is a set of ברייתות about acquiring, studied in לוי's study hall. It's not our מסכת קידושין.

phrases.english: if he locked, fenced, or breached even a little
in his presence – this is a חזקה.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי רַב הוֹשַׁעְיָא בְּקִדּוּשִׁין דְּבֵי לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא on the same small acts of acquiring, with an added condition
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Locking, fencing, or breaching even a little in the seller's presence is a חזקה.

steps.title: Does it not work when the seller is not there?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads an inference from the ברייתא: only in his presence does it work, but not when he is absent? That seems wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: In his presence, yes, it works. Not in his presence, it does not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's wording. It asks whether the act really fails when the seller is not standing there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An act of acquiring normally works no matter who is watching. So making the seller's presence a requirement seems strange, and the גמרא asks why that would be.

keyTerms.meaning: Not in his presence, when the seller is absent

phrases.english: In his presence – yes,
not in his presence – no?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges an inference from the ברייתא quoted in step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: The word בפניו in רב הושעיא's ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the act is only valid in the seller's presence, then it would fail when he is absent. But the buyer did the act either way, so why should it fail?

steps.title: רבא: in front of the seller, no permission needs to be said
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the ברייתא means: when the act is done in front of the seller, he does not need to say 'Go, take hold and acquire.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said, this is what it means: in his presence, he does not need to tell him, 'Go, take hold and acquire.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge by explaining what 'in his presence' is really about. His explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא says presence is not about whether the act works at all. It is about permission. When the seller watches and stays quiet, his agreement is clear, so he does not have to say out loud 'Go, take hold and acquire.'

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he means: an introduction to a new reading of a source
'Go, take hold and acquire': the seller's spoken permission to make the act of acquiring

phrases.english: Rava said, this is what it means:
In his presence – he does not need to say to him:
'Go, take hold and acquire,'
phrases.notes: The seller's watching shows he agrees, so no spoken permission is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16 by reading the ברייתא differently
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the ברייתא's wording (הכי קאמר)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'In his presence' seemed to mean the act only works when the seller is there.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'In his presence' means that no spoken permission is needed, because the seller's watching shows he agrees.
